summary: Describes a lightweight domain availability service using the Internet Registry Information Service framework and the data model of the IRIS domain registry service. It is on the standards track.

eli5.summary: This is a quick way to ask is this domain name taken, using the standard registry question system.

questions: how to check if a domain is available
how does iris check domain availability
what is the dchk1 application service label
subtitle: A lightweight IRIS service for asking whether a domain name is available, built as a strict subset of the DREG data model.

tldr.problem: Checking whether a domain name is available should be cheap and fast for high-volume, public-facing use, without exposing a full registration service.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 5144 defines the DCHK registry type for IRIS. Its data model is a strict subset of the DREG model, so a client asks about a domain name and gets back a small domain result with status information.
tldr.outcome: Operators can run DCHK in the same server process as DREG or separately, and users can follow a reference from an availability answer to full registration data.

today: RFC 5144 is a Proposed Standard from February 2008, and no RFC in the metadata obsoletes or updates it. It builds on the IRIS core protocol (RFC 3981) and the DREG type (RFC 3982).

sections.title: A Lightweight Availability Service
sections.content:
RFC 5144 describes a service for checking the availability of domain names. It is based on the IRIS framework (the Internet Registry Information Service, defined in RFC 3981) and uses the data model from RFC 3982, the IRIS Domain Registry (DREG) type. That gives the service IRIS features such as well-known methods for server navigation, structured queries and results, and layered extensibility.

The data model, called a registry schema in IRIS terms, is a strict subset of the DREG data model. The document says this lets implementors reuse DREG code paths. It also lets an operator run the service in the same server process as DREG (same host and port), in a different process on a different port, or on a different machine.
sections.eli5: It is like a shop with a quick 'is this in stock?' window next to the main counter. The window uses the same shelves as the counter but shows much less.

sections.title: Deployment and Relationship to DREG
sections.content:
Because DCHK is a subset of DREG, the two can sit side by side. The RFC gives an example: an operator might start with both services on the same machines, then later place the availability service on one set of machines and DREG on a separate set with a stricter set of controls. Either way, the change is transparent to the end user.

The service also fits together with DREG for the user. A person can find a domain's availability status and then reference the full registration information in DREG. When combined with the lightweight UDP transport of RFC 4993, the document calls the service lightweight and extremely efficient for high-volume, public-facing use.
sections.eli5: The quick window and the main counter can be in the same room or in different buildings. Either way, customers do not notice, and the window can point them to the counter for more.

sections.title: The Domain Result
sections.content:
The main result is a <domain> element representing an instance of a domain assignment. In the RFC's example it carries the attributes authority, registryType (here dchk1), entityClass and entityName, with a <domainName> child and a <status> child.

The children include <domainName>, which MUST be a domain name as specified by RFC 1035, and <idn>, the name in nameprep form where applicable. There are also <registrationReference>, which points to the downstream registration, and four date-time elements: <createdDateTime>, <initialDelegationDateTime>, <expirationDateTime> and <lastDatabaseUpdateDateTime>. An <iris:seeAlso> element can point to a related entity.

The <registrationReference> target MUST be a <domain> from this registry type or a <domain> as defined by RFC 3982. If a domain registry returns the result, it should point to the domain in the registrar or registrant service.
sections.eli5: The answer is a small card with the domain name, its status, and a few dates such as when it was created and when it expires. It can also say where to find the full file.

sections.title: Status Values and Queries
sections.content:
The <status> element holds child elements describing the domain's state. Examples are <active> (available via DNS, by delegation or direct publication), <inactive> (unavailable via DNS), <dispute> (the registrant assignment is in dispute) and <reserved> (not available for registration under normal procedures). Others cover grace periods from RFC 3915 (<addPeriod>, <renewPeriod>, <autoRenewPeriod>, <transferPeriod>, <redemptionPeriod>), policy compliance, operations such as <create>, <delete>, <renew>, <restore>, <transfer> and <update>, and <other> for system-specific states.

Each status can carry an optional <appliedDate>, an optional <ticket>, zero or more <description> elements (each MUST have a language attribute) and a <subStatus> with a required authority attribute. The optional attribute actor may be "registry", "registrar" or "registrationServiceProvider", and disposition may be "pending" or "prohibited".

For the IRIS <lookupEntity> query, two entity classes are recognized: domain-name and idn. Both yield a <domain> in the response.
sections.eli5: The status is like a sticker on the domain: free to use, on hold, being argued over, or reserved. You ask by name, and the registry answers with the sticker.

sections.title: Transports and URI Resolution
sections.content:
All DCHK clients and servers MUST implement the Lightweight UDP Transport Protocol (IRIS-LWZ, RFC 4993). Other transports are optional and at the server operator's discretion: XML Pipelining with Chunks (IRIS-XPC, RFC 4992) and BEEP (RFC 3983). The XPC transport is in any case preferable to BEEP. For BEEP, the registry type uses the default message pattern and the default server authentication method.

The application service label MUST be DCHK1, the abbreviated form of urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:dchk1. The bottom-up resolution method MUST be identified as bottom and the top-down method as top in IRIS URIs, and both work identically to the processes in RFC 3982.
sections.eli5: Every client and server must at least speak the simple, short-message way of talking. Fancier ways are optional, and the name tag for this service is DCHK1.

sections.title: Internationalization and IANA Registrations
sections.content:
Clients only need to localize the names of XML elements and attributes, plus the date and time elements. Results with internationalized data can include language information to help. All date and time elements use the XML Schema dateTime type, and UTC timestamps MUST use a capital Z.

IANA has registered the XML namespace urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:dchk1, the XML schema urn:ietf:params:xml:schema:dchk1, the S-NAPTR application service label DCHK1, and the BEEP profile URI http://iana.org/beep/iris1/dchk1.
sections.eli5: The names this service uses were written into an official list so nobody else picks the same ones.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC is short on this point. Because the registry is a proper subset of the DREG type in RFC 3982, it introduces no security considerations beyond those documented in RFC 3981, the IRIS core protocol.
sections.eli5: Since this service only shows a small part of what the bigger one shows, it needs no extra safety rules beyond the ones that already exist.
